# Deformation Field Parametrization

Also called: Dynamic NeRF deformation, Canonical space mapping, Time-varying radiance fields

## Overview
Deformation Field Parametrization addresses the limitation of static [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) (NeRFs) by enabling the representation of dynamic, non-rigid scenes. It solves the problem of reconstructing time-varying geometry and appearance by mapping 3D spatial coordinates and time into a static "canonical" space, where a standard static [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) can be applied [S1, unofficial][S2][S3, unofficial]. What sets this family apart from static [NeRF variants](#8585-specific-model-architectures.md) is the explicit modeling of temporal evolution through a deformation function, allowing for the reconstruction of moving objects from sparse or multi-view data that would otherwise be incoherent in a static model.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family rely on the differentiability of the forward rendering operator and the propagation of gradients through the integration steps [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]. The core mechanism is the evaluation of the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) and the computation of gradients with respect to scene parameters (density, geometry, transfer functions, camera poses) [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

The standard [emission-absorption model](#927-emission-absorption-model.md) computes the color $\hat{C}(\mathbf{r})$ for a ray $\mathbf{r}$ as [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]:

$$
\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)) \mathbf{c}_i
$$

where $\sigma_i$ is the density, $\delta_i$ is the step size, $\mathbf{c}_i$ is the color, and $T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$ is the transmittance [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

Differentiation strategies fall into three main categories [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]:
1. **Reverse-Mode [Automatic Differentiation](#7151-automatic-differentiation-reverse-adjoint-mode.md) (AD):** Standard backpropagation through the computational graph. This requires storing $O(kn)$ intermediate states (where $n$ is pixels and $k$ is samples), leading to high memory usage [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
2. **[Adjoint Method](#789-adjoint-method.md):** Computes gradients by propagating adjoint variables backward through the rendering algorithm, evaluating the chain rule from output to input. This has computational complexity largely constant in the number of parameters, making it preferable for optimizing many parameters like the transfer function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].
3. **Analytic Inversion / [Explicit Gradients](#7613-analytical-gradients.md):** Uses a-priori knowledge of the DVR operations to invert the order of operations or derive closed-form gradients, reducing memory consumption to $O(n)$ by avoiding the storage of intermediate results [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

The shared mathematical principle of deformation field parametrization is the transformation of a query point $\mathbf{x}_t$ at time $t$ to a canonical coordinate $\mathbf{x}_c$. This is typically achieved via a deformation function $f_{\Delta}$:
$$
\mathbf{x}_c = \mathbf{x}_t + \Delta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)
$$
or, when using inverse kinematics or skeleton-based methods, by combining inverse rigid transformations with neural displacement [S3, unofficial]. The canonical point $\mathbf{x}_c$ is then queried from a static radiance field $F_{\text{static}}$ to obtain density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$ [S1, S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Spline-based Deformation Field
A deformation field parametrization using cubic B-splines with time-modulated weights to map spatial coordinates $(x, y, z)$ at time $t$ to canonical coordinates $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, enabling reconstruction from sparse projections [S1, unofficial].

To implement this, one must calculate the deformation field from sparse few-projection data recorded at intermediate times $t$ during the dynamic experiment [S1, unofficial]. The full field spatio-temporal information is obtained by combining the canonical volume (fitted using rich many-projection data in pre-training steps via traditional computed tomography) and the calculated deformation field [S1, unofficial].

This method is chosen when data is extremely sparse (as few as two projections) and the scene topology remains constant [S1, unofficial]. Unlike methods using general MLP architectures for deformation fields which require complex regularization like elastic energy, this method uses cubic B-splines to enable reconstruction from minimal data [S1, unofficial].

A critical pitfall is that deformation fields based on canonical models fail when the scene topology changes over time, as they assume topology-preserving motion [S1, unofficial].

### Deformation-Guided Neural Fields
A method using deformation fields MLP guided by a morphable 3D face model to create a fully 3D face portrait with controllable pose and expression [S2].

This approach is chosen for animatable avatars and virtual humans where explicit control over facial expressions and pose is required [S2]. It builds on the paradigm of using a baseline skeleton equipped with an MLP-based deformation field, allowing for interpolation between frames and poses [S2].

### Neural Deformation Field
A neural network $F_{\Delta}$ that predicts per-point displacement $\Delta$ in canonical space to accommodate non-rigid deformation, conditioned on target pose $\theta_t$ and signed height $\tilde{h}$ [S3, unofficial].

The canonical point $\mathbf{x}_c$ is obtained by combining inverse Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) deformation and neural displacement:
$$
\mathbf{x}_c = LBS^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_t) + \Delta
$$
where $\Delta = F_{\Delta}(\phi(\tilde{h}), \theta_t)$ [S3, unofficial]. Here, $\phi(\cdot)$ represents a position encoding function [44-radiance-field-optimization.md], and $\tilde{h}$ is a signed height indicator derived from the signed distance $\bar{d}$ of the point to the mesh surface [S3, unofficial].

This method is chosen when joint optimization of geometry and texture is required without manual parameter tuning, allowing for editing of pose, geometry, and texture [S3, unofficial]. It specifically handles non-rigid deformation that LBS alone cannot capture [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of using canonical models and deformation fields originated in the context of [dynamic tomography](#7376-dynamic-tomographic-reconstruction-with-motion-identificatio.md) and neural rendering. Early approaches parametrized temporal evolution using discrete timesteps with linear interpolation or continuous grid displacements obtained from MLPs [S1, unofficial]. The drawback of canonical models is their inability to handle topological changes, which necessitates spatio-temporal networks or regularizers like elastic regularization, though these can be problematic for topological variations [S1, unofficial].

In the broader context of 3D vision, this paradigm was established for animating articulated bodies using a baseline skeleton with MLP-based deformation fields, inspiring works such as A-NeRF and Animatable NeRF [S2]. RigNeRF specifically innovated on this by using deformation fields guided by morphable 3D face models [S2]. More recent developments like UVA utilize neural deformation fields conditioned on pose and signed height to jointly optimize geometry fields from scratch [S3, unofficial].
